# OpenNitemare3D reimplementation of the 1994 FPS Nitemare 3D in C# [Twitter](https://twitter.com/CatboiN). [Discord](https://discord.gg/pr36YJ9Njw). [Tumblr](https://www.tumblr.com/blog/bbqgiraffe). # this is currently being rewritten in C for performance reasons, active development branch is C-Rewrite [![Showcase](https://yt-embed.herokuapp.com/embed?v=KLNquQF4iJo)](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=KLNquQF4iJo-Y "fucking uhhh") # how to compile: open the folder in vscode and press 'F5', you'll need the DotNet SDK this will compile and run fine on anything with DotNet and SFML # how to install: you will need to get the original game files, I reccomend just getting them from archive.org since the [version on David Gray's website](https://www.dgray.com/n3dpage.htm) is newer and has unsupported file types, however you will need to get SND.DAT from the newer version as the old version uses unsupported .VOC sounds [archive to newer version(you only need SND.DAT)](https://archive.org/download/win3_Nite3d3x/win3_Nite3d3x.zip), place SND.DAT(windows version!!!), UIF.DAT MAP.1, IMG.1, and GAME.PAL in bin/Debug/net5.0/data, then you can just launch the executable, it's untested on Windows but it should probably work since it's DotNet, you will probably need to download SFML binaries note that most of the menu options will crash the game, only new game and sound editor will do anything # how to help: if you for some reason want to contribute to my garbage you can join the discord, I'm open to any help especially with reverse engineering the executable as I'm garbage at assembly, I also need help labeling all the sound effects if you're David P Gray please consider open-sourcing Nitemare 3D ## features: * Loading of original bitmap images * Loading of original maps * Playback of MIDI music * Playback of SFX from Windows version (some Dos SFX *will* play but most of them sound garbage) * semi-functional main menu ## currently being worked on: * full support for Dos sound files * sprites * implementing curtains, warps, hidden panels * tile editor that auto-generates code for me ### file formats: #### DAT: Nitemare 3D uses the .DAT format(also used by David Gray in the Hugo series), this consists of a header that contains offsets for every file stored in the container, the offset consists of a unsigned 16 bit integer for the length followed by a unsiged 32 bit integer for the position.

files in SND.DAT consist of MIDI files followed by either 16 bit VOC or 8 bit PCM audio files(depending on the version). UIF.DAT consists of 256 color 320x200 PCX images #### MAP: maps are stored as text files and are very easy to read, the first 514 bytes are still unknown by me(could be tile definitions?) after that every map is stored as a 8192 byte chunk, every even byte is a tile id and every odd byte is a item id.

# RetroConverter v1.0.2

## What is it?

This is a converter for music files in .MOD format (Amiga Protracker
modules). It converts them to .RCM format meant to be used with the
[Retro Player](https://github.com/juusu/retro-player) playroutine.

It is an universal music format for the Amiga, with a (hopefully)
more flexible and reliable replay code than the original ProTracker
replay routine and variants.

## How do I use this?

You can use this tool either from your webbrowser or from the console.
The browser approach has the advantage that you don't need to install
any additional software, and you can also preview the converted tune
directly in the browser and check for any playback errors immideately!

The console approach might be more useful for coders, as you can make
the conversion a part of your build script, and have the uncoverted
.mod files in your project, which makes updating the music easier.

## Using the web UI:

You have two options:

### Build from source:

* clone this repository
* run: npm install
* run: npm run build
* open dist/index.html in your browser

(You'll need have NodeJS and npm installed on your machine for this to
work)

### Online UI:

Use the prebuilt online version at http://malimedo.com/rc/index.html

This doesn't send your music data to the server, all of the conversion 
happens client-side.

### Download prebuild web UI for offline use

If you'd rather use the web UI offline, head on over to the
[Releases](https://github.com/juusu/retro-convert/releases) page and
download the .zip with the latest version.

## Using from CLI:

You'll also need NodeJS installed to run the converter from CLI. Clone
the repo, and from the project folder run the following command:

node src\index-cli.js <mod_filename>

(where "mod_filename" is the name and path to the .MOD file to be
converted).

There are also some options you can pass to the command:

* --no-compress - Do not compress the track data - will result in very
                  large files, but they might compress better using an
                  .exe cruncher - could be useful for 4K intros or
                  similar
* --no-samples  - Do not save the sample data, can be useful if the
                  sample data will be generated with something like
                  4Klang or Cinter
* --no-sync     - Do not output sync data (8xx and E8x commands)
                  this might result in slightly smaller files if you
                  don't need sync data
* --debug       - Print (a lot of) additional info when compressing the
                  track data (probably not useful exept for debugging)

I'm also panning to find a way to build a standalone version of this
command which won't require NodeJS to run in future versions.

# Moonstone Rebuilt

An unofficial, fan-made enhancement of **Moonstone: A Hard Days Knight** (Mindscape, 1991; DOS version 1992) that
runs the original DOS game in DOSBox-X with bug fixes, automatic saves and better sound.

**This release contains no game files.** You need your own copy of the DOS version from GOG.com. The setup copies
your game files into this folder and patches the copies; your GOG installation is not changed.

## Requirements

### Mandatory
| What | Notes |
|---|---|
| **Moonstone: A Hard Days Knight, DOS version, from GOG.com** | The unchanged GOG release. The setup checks all 280 game files by checksum and stops if any is missing or different. Other releases (CD, floppy, other stores) are not supported yet. |
| **Windows 10 or 11** | The scripts are Windows batch and PowerShell files. |
| **DOSBox-X** | Tested with version 2026.10.01. `Start.bat` looks for `C:\DOSBox-X\dosbox-x.exe`, then `%ProgramFiles%\DOSBox-X`, then the `PATH`. Download: <https://dosbox-x.com/> |
| **Python 3.8 or newer** | Only for the setup. If Python does not have the package `unicorn`, the setup installs it with pip into the `_python` folder here (needs an internet connection once). Download: <https://www.python.org/downloads/> and tick *Add python.exe to PATH*. |

### Optional
| What | What it adds |
|---|---|
| **Your own Amiga Moonstone disk 1** as an ADF image | Richard Joseph's Amiga intro and ending music instead of the DOS tunes. See [Amiga music](#amiga-music-optional). |
| **VLC media player** | Needed once, to turn the Amiga music into WAV files. Not needed for playing. <https://www.videolan.org/> |
| **Roland MT-32 ROMs** (`MT32_CONTROL.ROM`, `MT32_PCM.ROM`, or the CM-32L ones) | The best DOS music. Put them in `mt32-roms`, then run `Music_MT32.bat`. Tested with MT-32 v1.07 (SHA-1 of `MT32_CONTROL.ROM`: `b083518fffb7f66b03c23b7eb4f868e62dc5a987`). They are Roland's copyright; obtain them legally. |
| **A General MIDI SoundFont** (e.g. the freely distributable *GeneralUser GS*, from <https://www.schristiancollins.com/generaluser.php>) | General MIDI music. Save it as `soundfonts\default.sf2`, then run `Music_GM.bat`. Tested with GeneralUser GS 2.0.3 (rename `GeneralUser-GS.sf2` to `default.sf2`); the GM profile uses the reverb and chorus settings its author recommends for DOSBox-X. |

The setup picks the music for you: MT-32 if the ROMs are there (the music was written for it), else General MIDI if
a SoundFont is there, else the original AdLib music. Put the files in place before running `Setup.bat`, or switch later with the `Music_*.bat` files.

## Installation

1. Install the game from GOG.com, DOSBox-X and Python 3.
2. Download this release and unpack it to a folder of its own, e.g. `C:\Games\Moonstone Rebuilt`.
3. Optional: put your Amiga disk image in the `amiga` folder (see below).
4. Run **`Setup.bat`**. It finds the GOG installation by itself (GOG Galaxy or the usual folders). If it does not,
   give the folder: `Setup.bat "D:\Games\GOG\Moonstone"`.
5. Start the game with **`Start.bat`**.

`Setup.bat` can be run again at any time, e.g. after adding the Amiga disk image. It leaves your saves (`save`),
ROMs and SoundFont alone.

## Amiga music (optional)

The Amiga version has two pieces of music, the intro and the ending, both on **disk 1**. They replace the DOS intro
and ending tunes; the music inside the game stays as chosen (the Amiga version has no in-game music).

* **File name and place:** save the image of your Amiga Moonstone **disk 1** as

  ```
  amiga\Moonstone_Disk1.adf
  ```

  inside this folder (the `amiga` folder is already there). Disks 2 and 3 are not needed.
* **Format:** a standard 880 KB AmigaDOS disk image (`.adf`), made from your own original disk, e.g. with a
  Greaseweazle or KryoFlux. The setup finds the music on the disk and reports if it differs from the known version.
* **Setup:** run `Setup.bat` (or `AmigaMusic_Setup.bat` if the game is already set up). It needs VLC once.
* **On and off:** `AmigaMusic_On.bat` / `AmigaMusic_Off.bat`.

While the Amiga music is on, the DOS intro and ending tunes are silent copies, and a small helper
(`amiga_music.ps1`) plays the Amiga music beside DOSBox-X while the intro or the ending runs. It stops when you
skip the intro.

## Playing

* **Start:** `Start.bat`.
* **Rules:** [GUIDE.md](GUIDE.md) is a player's guide written for Moonstone Rebuilt: the manual's topics plus the
  rules the manual leaves out, with notes where the manual and the game disagree.
* **Skip the intro or the ending:** Enter, Space or Esc.
* **Gold:** a knight can carry at most 150 gold. Anything above that is lost, and the game does not warn you.
* **Controls:** the arrow keys move; Enter + a direction attacks (when the knight faces right):

  | Direction + Enter | Move |
  |---|---|
  | up | overhead chop |
  | forward + up | upward thrust |
  | forward | swing |
  | forward + down | lunge |
  | down | sidestep (dodges thrusts and overhead chops) |
  | back + down | block |
  | back | backward thrust |
  | back + up | dagger throw |

  Second player: W, A, S and D (up, left, down, right) plus Tab. The original used X for down; Moonstone Rebuilt
  changes it to S (D9).
* **Practice:** with 1 player chosen in the menu, *Practice* is you against a Black Knight played by the computer
  (D11); with 2 players it is two players against each other, as in the original. With 3 or 4 players and one or
  two game controllers (D12-D14):
  * **Enter** on *Practice*: everyone against everyone until one knight is left, each in its own colour (blue,
    green, orange, red; with custom rules the colours of `[Knight1]`, `[Knight3]`, `[Knight2]` and `[Knight4]`).
  * **Space** on *Practice*: two teams, player 1 (arrows + Enter) with controller 1 against player 2 (W A S D +
    Tab) with controller 2, each team in its keyboard player's colour; teammates cannot hurt each other.
* **Practice against monsters** (D14, D15): in the first menu press a number. The monsters come as in their lair,
  several at a time. With 2-4 players chosen all the knights fight on the same side (3-4 need one or two game
  controllers, as above): they cannot hurt each other, every monster goes for the knight nearest to it, and the
  fight goes on while one knight stands; the knights' strength and hit points are added up, so more monsters come
  at a time. Esc ends a practice fight. `custom_rules.ini`, `[Practice]`, can give each key another lair (the list is there) and set whether
  knights or daggers hurt each other:

  | Key | Monsters | Key | Monsters |
  |---|---|---|---|
  | 1 | ratmen, 10 | 6 | spear troggs, 5 |
  | 2 | ratmen, 14 | 7 | Baloks, 3 |
  | 3 | wasteland troggs, 10 | 8 | mudmen, 5 |
  | 4 | axe troggs, 10 | 9 | trolls, 6 |
  | 5 | war beasts, 9 | 0 | the Black Knight |

  Two controllers: see *Game controllers*.
* **Give up (Game Over):** Esc on the map. In the original game this was Q, next to the second player's keys, so a
  game could end by accident; Moonstone Rebuilt moves it to Esc (fix K5). It does not ask first.
* **Quit DOSBox-X:** Ctrl+F9 (asks first) or close the window.

### Game controllers

The DOS game reads the PC joystick port, and DOSBox-X turns a modern USB or Bluetooth controller (Xbox, PlayStation,
most generic gamepads) into that joystick. Nothing needs installing:

1. Run the script for your controllers, once:
   * `Controller_PlayStation.bat`: PlayStation pads (tested with PS3 pads; their stick reports up and down reversed,
     which this turns round).
   * `Controller_Standard.bat`: Xbox and most other pads.

   Both turn the D-pad on as well as the left stick and give each player a controller of their own (player 1 the
   first, player 2 the second; also for 3-4 player practice). `Controller_Default.bat` goes back to DOSBox-X's own
   bindings, with one controller for both players (its right stick and its third and fourth buttons are player 2).
2. Connect the controllers **before** `Start.bat`; DOSBox-X looks for controllers only when it starts.
3. Each player moves with the left stick or the D-pad and attacks with the first or second button (A or B on an Xbox
   pad; cross or circle on a PlayStation pad). The keyboard keeps working alongside.
4. If the knight drifts or ignores a direction, calibrate: on the game's first menu press **J**, then follow the
   two screens (stick to the top left + button, stick to the bottom right + button). If up and down are the wrong
   way round, run the other of the two scripts.

The scripts copy a file from `controllers` to `moonstone.map` (DOSBox-X's bindings) and set `joysticktype` in
`moonstone-dosbox-x.conf`; a `moonstone.map` of your own is kept as `moonstone.map.bak`.

**Your own bindings.** DOS games see only the sticks (two axes and two buttons per controller); everything else is
bound in DOSBox-X's mapper: start the game, press **F11+M** (*Main → Mapper editor*), click an arrow of joystick 1
or 2 or a key, then **Add** and press the controller's button or direction (**Del** removes the selected binding).
Click **Save**, then **Exit**; the bindings stay in `moonstone.map`. This way the other buttons can do Space (the
inventory) or E (end the turn). If the stick still drifts, raise `joy1deadzone1` (default 0.25) under `[joystick]`.

### Saving and loading
* **Your own saves:** F11+S saves and F11+L loads, using the slot chosen under *Capture → Select save slot*
  (slot 1 by default; there are 100).
* **Automatic saves:** the game pauses for about a second and saves
  * at the start of every human player's turn on the map: slots **91–95**, shown as `PRETURN`
  * at the start of every fight: slots **96–100**, shown as `PREFIGHT`.

  Computer knights' turns are not saved. Both ranges rotate; one turn or fight often fills two slots with the same
  moment, so each range holds roughly the last two or three.
* **Loading an automatic save:** *Capture → Select save slot* → go to the last page (slots 91–100) → pick the newest
  slot by its time → *Capture → Load state* (or F11+L). Before saving by hand again, select slot 1 (or another slot
  below 91), or the next automatic save will overwrite yours.

## Options

| File | Does |
|---|---|
| `Music_AdLib.bat` / `Music_GM.bat` / `Music_MT32.bat` | Music version. If the ROMs or the SoundFont are missing, `Start.bat` falls back to AdLib. |
| `SoundCard_SoundBlaster.bat` / `SoundCard_AdLib.bat` | Sound effects as digitised samples (Sound Blaster, default) or on the AdLib synthesiser. |
| `Fixes_On.bat` / `Fixes_Off.bat` | All fixes (default) or the original game: the original programs (only unpacked, so that they run in DOSBox-X) and sound files. Saves do not carry over between the two. In original mode there are no automatic saves. |
| `AmigaMusic_On.bat` / `AmigaMusic_Off.bat` | Amiga intro and ending music on or off (after it has been set up). |
| `Custom_rules_on.bat` / `Custom_rules_off.bat` / `Custom_rules_reset.bat` | Use the custom rules in `custom_rules.ini`, use the default rules (the normal game), or restore `custom_rules.ini` to the default state (`custom_rules-default.ini`) (D10). Restart DOSBox-X after a change. `Custom_rules_on.bat` needs Python. |
| `custom_rules.ini` | The custom rules: each knight's starting abilities, life points, hit points, gold, weapon, armour and items, what happens when it dies, the computer knights' extras, and global rules (disease, curses, gold and life caps, home village, E key, moon, weapon damage, armour hit points). Every setting is explained in the file. |
| `moonstone-dosbox-x.conf` | DOSBox-X settings: window size, shader, speed, saves. |

### Custom rules (`custom_rules.ini`)

`custom_rules.ini` changes the game without touching the fixes. It comes with the normal game's values: edit it, run `Custom_rules_on.bat` and restart DOSBox-X. `Custom_rules_off.bat` goes back to the default rules, and `Custom_rules_reset.bat` restores `custom_rules.ini` to the default state from `custom_rules-default.ini` (leave that file as it is). Every setting lists its allowed values; values above the normal game's limits are allowed, and the bounds only keep the game from breaking. `Custom_rules_on.bat` checks every value before it changes anything. Keep a copy of your `custom_rules.ini` when you install a newer Moonstone Rebuilt over this folder. The main settings:

* **Per knight** (`[Knight1]`–`[Knight4]` in the order of the selection screen: Sir Godber, Sir Richard, Sir Jeffrey and Sir Edward; `[Black]` for every knight the computer plays): the home village (where the knight starts, respawns and is healed; two knights can share one), strength, constitution, endurance, life points, extra hit points, gold, experience, daggers, weapon, armour, how many of each magic item, keys and Moonstones, and its colour: blue, orange, green, red, black or any colour as `#RGB` (e.g. `#80F`). The colour is only how the knight is drawn, so any combination works; on the map a `#RGB` knight shows as the nearest of the five named colours, and the selection screen keeps the original portraits.
* **Death mode per knight:** `permadeath` (the original), `reincarnation` (starts again from its starting values at its start), `respawn` (back at its start with full life points, keeps the rest) or `invulnerable` (never loses the last life point; a winner still takes items).
* **Saves:** `save_mode` = `autosave_and_manual` (as before), `autosave_only`, `manual_only` or `none`. DOSBox-X still takes F11+S, but with `autosave_only` or `none` loading such a save stops the game at the next turn, fight or roll, with LOADAUTO or NOSAVES in the title bar. `prevent_savescumming = on`: loading a save does not change how the tavern dice, Math, Mythral and the scroll curses turn out.
* **Computer knights:** experience every moon phase, the free visit to Math the Wizard, experience for a duel win.
* **Global:** ratmen disease, curse chances, gold and life caps, home village healing (`below_3`, `below_max`, `full`; only in the knight's own village or in any village), full hit points with the E key, days per moon phase, experience per ability point, the damage each weapon adds and the hit points each armour and Ring of Protection adds (as in the game, armour does not reduce damage), the base damage of each move including the dagger throw, the most daggers a knight can carry.
* **Treasure, Math and Mythral:** the dragon's hoard (`grows` with its victories, `reset` each game, or `keep` as the original), what the lairs hold (gold, magic items or both), the gold amount, the chance of each magic item (lairs, Math, the dragon's hoard and the High Temple's stock), what Math the Wizard gives and his frog days and irritation, and Mythral's chance of success for each size of donation. Tables the game could roll on forever (for example only one kind of magic item) are refused.
* **Practice:** what each practice key 1-0 starts (monster type or the Black Knight, the lair's ground, monsters to defeat, how many at once), whether knights' blows and daggers hurt other knights, and whether monsters go for the nearest knight or the first.
* **Monsters:** the hit points and damage of every monster, the ratmen by moon phase, the Guardian and the dragon, and the least damage the dragon does against Talismans of the Wyrm.
* **Prices:** the weapon and armour shops (the computer knights pay the same), the healer and every High Temple item. The prices on screen follow; selling at the temple pays half, as in the game.
* **Selling at the merchant** (`merchant_selling = on`): click one of your daggers, your weapon or your armour on the merchant screen to sell it for half its price, rounded down. You get the long sword or padded armour back for free; armour takes its hit points with it, and chain mail and battle armour their extra movement. Magic items, the Sword of Sharpness included, are not bought there.

The starting values apply to a new game; a running game or a save state keeps the knights it has. The custom rules work only with the fixes on (`Fixes_On.bat`).

## What is changed

All changes are listed with details in **[FIXES.md](FIXES.md)**. In short:

* **Bug fixes:** the hidden ratmen disease that took a life point every four days is gone; duel loot no longer
  duplicates the Sword of Sharpness; the game no longer ends
  when Q is pressed by accident (Game Over is now on Esc); Math the Wizard
  and Mythral raise the right stats and say the right thing; fights can no longer run
  out of object slots; the sound effects play at their real speed; a sound that never played now
  plays; ratmen grow stronger with the moon as the manual says.
* **Improvements:** optional custom rules in `custom_rules.ini` (starting values per knight, death modes, caps and more); automatic saves before every fight and turn; the intro and ending can be skipped; the intro
  works in DOSBox-X; MT-32, General MIDI or AdLib music; optional Amiga intro and ending music; DOSBox-X settings
  from the GOG community (speed, joystick, black screen); 4:3 picture with crisp pixels.

The original difficulty and rules are kept.

## Known limitations

* Some fixes are worked out from the game code and not yet confirmed in play; [FIXES.md](FIXES.md) says which.
* The Amiga music starts with the intro program, so it is not in step with the DOS intro's pictures, and DOSBox-X's
  volume setting does not affect it.
* An automatic save often takes two slots (DOSBox-X's save pauses the game's wait).
* The mouse is turned off: the game does not use it, and a captured mouse disturbed the intro's keyboard handling.

## Troubleshooting

| Problem | What to do |
|---|---|
| *The GOG installation of Moonstone was not found* | Give the folder: `Setup.bat "path\to\Moonstone"`. |
| *game files are missing or different* | Verify or reinstall the game in GOG Galaxy. Only the unchanged GOG DOS release works. |
| *Python 3.8 or newer is needed* | Install Python 3 with *Add python.exe to PATH* ticked, then run `Setup.bat` again. The setup tries the `py` launcher first and then `python`, and uses the first that starts. |
| *custom_rules.ini: ... Nothing was changed* | `Setup.bat` checks the custom rules before it changes anything: correct the value it names (or run `Custom_rules_off.bat` or `Custom_rules_reset.bat`), then run `Setup.bat` again. |
| *DOSBox-X was not found* | Install DOSBox-X to `C:\DOSBox-X` or add it to the `PATH`. |
| No music | Normal on the map and in fights: the game only has music in the intro, the ending and five places. If it is silent there too, run `Music_AdLib.bat`. |
| No sound effects as samples | Run `SoundCard_SoundBlaster.bat`. |
| The game freezes at the first fight or turn, or when taking a weapon after a duel | `SAVEHOOK.COM` is not running; run `Setup.bat` again. As a workaround, `Fixes_Off.bat`. |
| *custom_rules.ini: ... must be ...* when running `Custom_rules_on.bat` | A value in `custom_rules.ini` is out of bounds, misspelt or missing; the message names it and its allowed values. Nothing was changed. `Custom_rules_reset.bat` starts again from the defaults. |
| The game stops and the title bar says LOADAUTO or NOSAVES | `custom_rules.ini` has `save_mode = autosave_only` or `none`, and a save made with F11+S was loaded. Load the newest automatic save (slots 91–100) with `autosave_only`; with `none` start a new game. |
| The game freezes when a new game starts, after `Custom_rules_on.bat` | DOSBox-X was not restarted, so the old `SAVEHOOK.COM` is still running. Restart DOSBox-X. |

## Credits and legal

*Moonstone: A Hard Days Knight* was designed by Rob Anderson and Todd Prescott, with music by Richard Joseph,
published by Mindscape; the DOS version is sold by GOG.com. Moonstone Rebuilt is an unofficial fan project and is

It runs in CI on every push and pull request. No automatic check can guarantee that nothing slips through; it is a safety net, not a substitute for looking at what you commit. --- ## What is this? retro-native is a **standard, a shared SDL2 shell, a CRT shader and a packaging template** for turning *one* old game into a self-contained, native-feeling PC game: - the player double-clicks an icon (or installs a package) and sees **the game**, not a launcher, a frontend or an emulator configuration screen; - one game = one repository = one binary per OS, with the (owner's own) game data baked in; - sensible defaults for everything, so nobody has to know what the original platform was. They just want their one favourite game from back then to be playable like any other PC game. ## How it works There are two routes, both using the same shell and the same user experience. **Route A - libretro core, statically linked.** A libretro core (C64, NES, SNES, Mega Drive, Amiga, DOS via DOSBox, ...) is linked statically into the game binary together with `shell/`. The shell provides window, video, audio, input, menu, settings and save slots; a small set of per-game hooks (`src/game/` in the game repository) provides the title, default key map, core options, the data to load, boot handling and mouse/port quirks. # SwosGfx
Tool for generating or extracting graphics data and palettes for SWOS (Amiga and DOS).

### Screenshots

![](images/tiled_00.png)

![](images/tiled_01.png)

---

## Amiga usage

### Explicit input/output (two positional args)

```bash
SwosGfx -amiga -map -output=bmp  [-palette=<name>] [-bitplanes=N] [-no-rnc] in.map out.bmp
SwosGfx -amiga -map -output=tmj  [-palette=<name>] [-bitplanes=N] [-no-rnc] in.map out.tmj
SwosGfx -amiga -tmj -output=map  [-bitplanes=N]    [-no-rnc]      in.tmj out.map
SwosGfx -amiga -bmp -output=map  [-bitplanes=N]    [-no-rnc]      fullPitch.bmp out.map
SwosGfx -amiga -bmp -output=raw  [-palette=<name>] [-bitplanes=N] [-no-rnc] in.bmp out.raw
SwosGfx -amiga -raw -output=bmp  [-palette=<name>] [-bitplanes=N] [-no-rnc] in.raw out.bmp
````

### Batch mode (0 or 1 positional arg)

In batch mode, input comes from the Amiga directory (`./Amiga` by default, or `-amiga-dir=<path>`).

* **0 args**: output goes to the current directory
* **1 arg**: treated as an output directory

Supported batch conversions:

```bash
SwosGfx -amiga -raw -output=bmp  [-palette=<name>] [-bitplanes=N] [-no-rnc] [outDir]
SwosGfx -amiga -map -output=bmp  [-palette=<name>] [-bitplanes=N] [-no-rnc] [outDir]
SwosGfx -amiga -map -output=tmj  [-palette=<name>] [-bitplanes=N] [-no-rnc] [outDir]
```

---

## DOS usage

### DOS pitch rendering (patterns from `./DOS`)

In DOS pitch mode, input is implicit from the DOS directory (`./DOS` by default, or `-dos-dir=<path>`).

This mode renders **all 6 pitches** (`pitch1..pitch6`) using the selected type.

* **0 args**: output goes to the current directory
* **1 arg**: treated as an output directory

```bash
SwosGfx -dos -output=bmp [-pitch=N] [-type=normal] [-colors=N] [outDir]
SwosGfx -dos -output=tmj [-pitch=N] [-type=normal] [-colors=N] [-insertblanktile] [-tilesetwidth=N] [outDir]
```

Output filenames:

* BMP: `pitchN-<type>.bmp`
* Tiled: `pitchN-<type>.tmj` plus `pitchN-<type>.bmp`, its 8bpp tileset image

Where `<type>` is one of: `frozen, muddy, wet, soft, normal, dry, hard`.

Note: `-pitch` currently exists as an option, but the current implementation renders pitches `1..6` in a loop.

#### Tiled (`.tmj`) export

A pitch is a 42x55 grid of 16x16 patterns, so `-output=tmj` writes the real tile map
rather than a flattened picture: one tile layer plus a tileset image with the unique
tiles. Maps are written in [Tiled's JSON map format](https://doc.mapeditor.org/en/stable/reference/json-map-format/)
(`.tmj`) - one orthogonal tile layer, one embedded tileset with an external image, and
the tile data as a plain array of GIDs. `-output=json` and `-output=tmx` are accepted as
aliases and produce the same `.tmj` file.

On input the format is detected from the file content rather than its extension, so the
XML `.tmx` maps SwosGfx wrote before the switch still load (`-tmj`, `-json` and `-tmx`
are all the same input switch).

Patterns are deduplicated on pixel content, and the switches match the ones
[Tiled2Bin](https://github.com/benbaker76/Tiled2Bin) uses for its `-slice` mode:

| Option              | Description                                                                                                   | Default |
| ------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------- |
| `-insertblanktile`  | Reserve tile id 0 for an all-transparent tile, so the map never contains gid 0 ("no tile").                    | `false` |
| `-tilesetwidth=<n>` | Tileset image width in pixels (must be a multiple of 16). `256` gives the usual 16 tiles across.               | `256`   |

`!Extract_DOS_Pitches_Tiled.bat` (in `bin/Debug/net8.0`) renders all 7 pitch types with
`-insertblanktile` into `DOS_Pitches_Tiled`. The maps round-trip: feeding one back
through `-amiga -tmj -output=map` reproduces the pitch pixel for pixel.

---

### DOS picture usage (`.256` → BMP)

```bash
SwosGfx -dos -picture -output=bmp in.256 out.bmp
```

---

### DOS sprite usage (SPRITE.DAT + *.DAT from `./DOS`)

#### Export all sprites to BMP

* **0 args**: output to current directory
* **1 arg**: treated as output directory

```bash
SwosGfx -dos -sprites-export [-sprite-bg=N] [-output=bmp] [outDir]
# writes sprNNNN.bmp, 0 <= N < 1334
```

#### Import sprites from a directory and update DAT/SPRITE.DAT

```bash
SwosGfx -dos -sprites-import spritesDir
# reads sprNNNN.bmp, inserts and saves changes to DAT/SPRITE.DAT
```

---

### DOS → Amiga bank conversion (`-dos2amiga`)

Rebuilds the Amiga sprite / menu / charset banks from the **DOS** graphics: each DOS
sprite is placed at the exact position the original Amiga bank uses (read from the SWOS
image-command scripts), and the result is written as an 8bpp indexed BMP using the DOS
palette. This is the inverse of how the game extracts sprites from a bank.

```bash
SwosGfx -dos -dos2amiga [outDir]
```

Produces 11 banks:

* **Gameplay** (Game palette): `CJCGRAFS`, `CJCTEAM1`, `CJCTEAM2`, `CJCTEAM3`, `CJCTEAMG`, `CJCBITS`, `SOCCER_S`, `CJCBENCH`
* **Menu / charset** (Menu palette): `CHARSET`, `MENUS`, `MENUS2`

DOS sprite indices map to Amiga indices as `Amiga = DOS − 114` for gameplay sprites
(DOS index ≥ 227) and 1:1 for the menu / charset sprites. `CJCTEAM1/2/3` share one
layout, sourced from `TEAM1/TEAM2/TEAM3.DAT` respectively; `SOCCER_S` (the big R/S
rotation) uses palette slots `0x70..0x7F`. Full-screen images with no DOS equivalent
(`LOADER*`, `DISK22`, `OLDDISK1`, `MENUBG*`, `RAINBOW`) are not produced by this mode.

---

### Jaguar → Amiga bank conversion (`-jag2amiga`)

The Atari Jaguar release (*Sensible Soccer International Edition*, 1995) ships its
in-game artwork as nine LZ-packed `*.lzj` blobs, each unpacking to exactly 81920 bytes =
one 320x256 8bpp sheet. Six of those sheets are the gameplay sprite banks, laid out at
the **same pixel coordinates** the Amiga image-command scripts read from - the Jaguar
port kept the Amiga bank layout and simply redrew the art at 256 colours.

So this is `-dos2amiga` with a different pixel source: the same scripts are walked, but
each placement is lifted straight out of the matching Jaguar sheet. SwosGfx reads the
cartridge itself (it has its own `lz-bits` depacker and CRY colour conversion), so no
external tooling is needed.

```bash
SwosGfx -dos -jag2amiga [-jag-rom=<path>] [-jag-dir=<path>] [outDir]
```

With no `-jag-rom`, the first `*.jag` / `*.j64` / `*.rom` / `*.bin` in `./Jag` is used.
The DOS directory is still required - it supplies everything the Jaguar release lacks.

| Amiga bank                          | Jaguar stream | Source                                                     |
| ----------------------------------- | ------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------- |
| `CJCGRAFS`                          | `$8947C0`     | Jaguar scoreboard font + clock captions only, rest from DOS |
| `CJCTEAM1`                          | `$8AC828`     | Jaguar (303 / 303 with the celebration art)                 |
| `CJCTEAM2`                          | `$8AFB58`     | Jaguar (303 / 303)                                          |
| `CJCTEAM3`                          | `$8B2FE0`     | Jaguar (303 / 303)                                          |
| `CJCTEAMG`                          | `$8A02E8`     | Jaguar (232 / 232 - exact)                                  |
| `CJCBITS`                           | `$8993D8`     | Jaguar (24 / 30)                                            |
| `CJCBENCH`                          | `$89D0B0`     | Jaguar (58 / 61)                                            |
| `SOCCER_S`, `CHARSET`, `MENUS`, `MENUS2` | -        | DOS - the Jaguar has its own menu system                    |

Anything the Jaguar sheets do not hold falls back to the DOS sprite, so the output is a
complete drop-in set.

#### Celebration frames

The one gap in the Jaguar artwork is the goal **celebration** - Amiga sprites `251-256`,
`352-357` and `453-458`, which all point at the same six cells at `(144,64)`-`(176,80)`.
That whole 48x32 block is blank in all three Jaguar team sheets, because the Jaguar game
has no celebration. It is supplied by hand-drawn Jaguar-style art:

```
Jag/CJCTEAM1_CELEB.bmp
Jag/CJCTEAM2_CELEB.bmp
Jag/CJCTEAM3_CELEB.bmp
```

Each is a 48x32 8bpp BMP - the bank block at `(144,64)`, a 3x2 grid of 16x16 cells whose
top-left corners hold the six 12x15 sprites (the last is 11x15). It is stamped onto the
sheet before the script walk, so the frames flow through the normal placement path and
all three kit banks come out **303 / 303 from the Jaguar**, with no DOS fallback at all.

Draw against the Jaguar palette (`JAG_GAME.act`, written next to the converted banks);
art in another palette still works, it is matched onto the nearest Jaguar colours on the
way in. Delete a `_CELEB.bmp` and that bank reverts to the DOS celebration sprites.

Banks are written in the Jaguar in-game CRY palette (`$6FA42` in the cartridge), dumped
next to them as `JAG_GAME.act`; DOS fallback sprites are remapped from the DOS Game
palette onto the nearest Jaguar colours so each bank stays a single 256-colour image.
The banks with no Jaguar source at all keep their DOS palette.

`!Convert_Jag_to_Amiga.bat` (in `bin/Debug/net8.0`) runs the whole thing into
`Amiga_Images_256_Jag`. Put the cartridge image in `Jag\`, or pass its path as the first
argument. The ROM is not distributed with SwosGfx.

---

## DOS → Amiga AGA build (`!DOS2AGA.bat`)

`!DOS2AGA.bat` (in `bin/Debug/net8.0`) converts the DOS graphics into a complete Amiga
**AGA** set in `Amiga_AGA`, ready for the AGA port:

1. `-raw -output=bmp -colors=256` — Amiga-only full-screen images (loaders / backgrounds)
2. `-dos -dos2amiga` — rebuild the 11 sprite / menu / charset banks from the DOS graphics
3. `-dos -output=bmp -colors=256` — render the DOS pitches
4. `-bmp -output=raw -bitplanes=auto` — pack each bank to RAW (4bpp or 8bpp, see below)
5. `-bmp -output=map -bitplanes=8` — pack the DOS pitches to AGA MAP

### Bit depth per file (`-bitplanes=auto`)

`-bitplanes=auto` picks the smallest depth that fits each image: **4bpp** if it only
uses palette indices 0–15, otherwise **8bpp**. Because the DOS sprites are natively 4bpp,
most banks stay 4bpp (half the size) instead of storing empty upper planes — only art
that genuinely needs the higher palette entries is written as 8bpp.

| Output | Depth | Reason |
| ------ | :---: | ------ |
| `CHARSET`, `MENUS`, `MENUS2` | **4bpp** | menu / charset sprites, colours 0–15 |
| `CJCGRAFS`, `CJCTEAM1`, `CJCTEAM2`, `CJCTEAM3`, `CJCTEAMG`, `CJCBITS`, `CJCBENCH` | **4bpp** | gameplay sprites, colours 0–15 |
| `SOCCER_S` | **8bpp** | big R/S rotation uses palette `0x70..0x7F` |
| `MENUBG`, `MENUBG2` | **8bpp** | background, colours sit at high indices |
| `DISK22`, `OLDDISK1` | **8bpp** | remapped to the 256-colour palette |
| `LOADER00`–`LOADER10`, `LOADER76`, `LOADER8A`, `LOADER8B` | **8bpp** | remapped to the 256-colour palette |
| `RAINBOW` | **8bpp** | full 256-colour image |
| `SWCPICH1`–`SWCPICH6` (pitches) | **8bpp** | 256-colour tiles |

> **Palettes are not baked into the RAW/MAP** (they store indices only). The AGA port
> supplies the 256-colour DOS palette: the **Menu** palette for `CHARSET`/`MENUS`/`MENUS2`
> and the **Game** palette for the gameplay banks and pitches. RAW/MAP output stays
> RNC-compressed (add `-no-rnc` for uncompressed).

### Extended font (`-font-extend`)

`!DOS2AGA.bat` runs the font extender on `CHARSET.bmp` (after `-dos2amiga`, before the RAW
conversion) to draw the full-ASCII + accented glyphs into the sheet's free cells:

```bash
SwosGfx -font-extend [-glyphs=glyphs.txt] charset.bmp [out.bmp]
```

* The glyph shapes come from **`glyphs.txt`** (`*`=ink, `-`=blank; one `@<char> <small|big>`
  block per glyph). Edit it to **add / remove / change** glyphs; the 1px drop-shadow
  (palette index 8) is added automatically.
* New glyphs go into the free 16×8 cells (small font top half, big font bottom half) from
  sprite slot **1220**, matching the game's `font_ext_script.inc`.
* The input **palette is preserved** (indices 2=white, 8=shade), so it works for both the
  **AGA** CHARSET (DOS palette, from `-dos2amiga`) and an **OCS** CHARSET (Amiga palette).
  Omit `out.bmp` to overwrite in place.
* Empty cells in rows 0–27 are filled with the **"missing glyph" box** (the ⊠ marker the
  stock Amiga charset draws in unused cells); rows 28–31 stay blank. Pass `-no-boxes` to
  skip this. Cells that already hold a glyph or box are left untouched.
* An **`integration.txt`** (image-script + conversionTable wiring) is written next to
  `glyphs.txt` — apply it to the game side if you change `glyphs.txt`, so the extraction
  positions stay in sync.

---

## Directories

* Amiga graphics files: `./Amiga` (default, can be changed with `-amiga-dir=<path>`)

  * Pitch files: `SWCPICH1.MAP`, `SWCPICH2.MAP`, `SWCPICH3.MAP`, `SWCPICH4.MAP`, `SWCPICH5.MAP`, `SWCPICH6.MAP`, `SWCPICH7.MAP`
  * Raw files: `CHARSET.RAW`, `CJCBENCH.RAW`, `CJCBITS.RAW`, `CJCGRAFS.RAW`, `CJCTEAM1.RAW`, `CJCTEAM2.RAW`, `CJCTEAM3.RAW`, `CJCTEAMG.RAW`, `DISK22.RAW`, `LOADER00.RAW`, `LOADER01.RAW`, `LOADER1.RAW`, `LOADER10.RAW`, `LOADER2.RAW`, `LOADER3.RAW`, `LOADER4.RAW`, `LOADER5.RAW`, `LOADER6.RAW`, `LOADER7.RAW`, `LOADER8A.RAW`, `LOADER8B.RAW`, `LOADER9.RAW`, `MENUBG.RAW`, `MENUBG2.RAW`, `MENUS.RAW`, `MENUS2.RAW`, `OLDDISK1.RAW`, `SOCCER_S.RAW`

* DOS graphics files: `./DOS` (default, can be changed with `-dos-dir=<path>`)

  * Pitch maps: `PITCH1.DAT`, `PITCH2.DAT`, `PITCH3.DAT`, `PITCH4.DAT`, `PITCH5.DAT`, `PITCH6.DAT`
  * Pitch data: `PITCH1.BLK`, `PITCH2.BLK`, `PITCH3.BLK`, `PITCH4.BLK`, `PITCH5.BLK`, `PITCH6.BLK`
  * Picture files: `TITLE.256`, `SCORES.256`, `LOADSCR.256`
  * Sprite files: `SPRITE.DAT`, `CHARSET.DAT`, `SCORE.DAT`, `TEAM1.DAT`, `TEAM3.DAT"`, `GOAL1.DAT`, `GOAL1.DAT`, `BENCH.DAT`

* Jaguar assets: `./Jag` (default, can be changed with `-jag-dir=<path>`)

  * Cartridge image: `Sensible Soccer International Edition (1995).jag` (2,097,152 bytes), or point at one elsewhere with `-jag-rom=<path>`. Not distributed with SwosGfx.
  * Celebration art: `CJCTEAM1_CELEB.bmp`, `CJCTEAM2_CELEB.bmp`, `CJCTEAM3_CELEB.bmp` (48x32, 8bpp)

## Map Data (Amiga)

The Amiga map format consists of a 42 x 55 tile map followed immediately by the tile pixel data. The tile map is an array of 32-bit values, one per tile cell (42 * 55 = 2310 entries, 9240 bytes total). Each entry stores an offset (byte address) into the tile data block for the tile that should be drawn at that cell. In other words, the map does not store "tile indices" in the conventional sense; it stores pointers/offsets to the tile’s pixel payload within the tile data that follows.

Directly after the 9240-byte tile map comes the tile data itself, stored as a contiguous stream of 16 x 16 pixel tiles in classic Amiga planar (bitplane) format using 4 bitplanes (16 colors). Each tile is encoded one scanline at a time: for each of the 16 rows, the data contains one 16-bit word per bitplane (because 16 pixels / 16 bits = 1 word). The planes are stored separately, and the final pixel color index is reconstructed by taking the corresponding bit from each plane (plane 0 is the least-significant bit), combining them into a 4-bit value in the range 0-15. This yields a per-tile storage size of 16 rows x 4 planes x 2 bytes = 128 bytes per tile, and the map entry offsets point to the start of these 128-byte tile records within the tile data stream.

### Bit depth and the offset unit

A MAP does not record its own bit depth, so `-bitplanes=N` has to match the file. Get it
wrong and SwosGfx says so, and lists the depths the tile data would actually divide into —
the AGA pitches in `Amiga/`, for example, are 7 bitplanes (224 bytes per tile), not 4.

Two conventions for the map entries exist in the wild. SwosGfx writes a true byte offset,
`tileIndex * 16 * bitplanes * 2`, but AGA pitches also exist whose entries keep the original
OCS scaling of a fixed **128 bytes per tile** whatever the real depth is — at 4 bitplanes the
two are the same number, which is why the difference is easy to miss. Reading works out which
one a file uses by checking the whole table against both (a unit only fits if every entry is a
multiple of it *and* lands on a tile that exists), so either loads without a switch.

### More Amiga examples

```bash

SwosGfx -amiga -bmp -output=map -bitplanes=4 fullPitch.bmp SWCPICH1.MAP

SwosGfx -amiga -raw -output=bmp -palette=Normal -bitplanes=4 pitch.raw pitch-normal.bmp

# Convert a Tiled map back to Amiga .MAP (7 bitplanes for AGA)
SwosGfx -amiga -tmj -output=map -bitplanes=7 pitch1-aga.tmj SWCPICH1.MAP
```

### More DOS examples

```bash
SwosGfx -dos -picture -output=bmp TITLE.256 title-screen.bmp

SwosGfx -dos -sprites-export -dos-dir=DOS -sprite-bg=0 sprites-out

SwosGfx -dos -sprites-import sprites-out
```

### DOS Tiled examples

```bash
# Render all DOS pitches, SOFT type, directly to Tiled .tmj maps
SwosGfx -dos -dos-dir=DOS -output=tmj -type=soft -colors=128 pitches-soft-tiled

SwosGfx -dos -dos-dir=DOS -output=tmj -type=dry -colors=256 pitches-dry-256-tiled

# Render all DOS pitches, NORMAL type, with a blank tile at id 0 (Tiled2Bin -slice style)
SwosGfx -dos -dos-dir=DOS -output=tmj -insertblanktile -type=normal DOS_Pitches_Tiled

# Same, but with a 32-tile-wide tileset image instead of 16
SwosGfx -dos -dos-dir=DOS -output=tmj -insertblanktile -tilesetwidth=512 -type=normal DOS_Pitches_Tiled
```

```bash
# Rebuild the Amiga banks from a Jaguar cartridge sitting in ./Jag
SwosGfx -dos -dos-dir=DOS -jag2amiga Amiga_Images_256_Jag

SwosGfx -dos -dos-dir=DOS -jag2amiga "-jag-rom=D:\roms\Sensible Soccer International Edition (1995).jag" Amiga_Images_256_Jag
```

```bash
# Convert an Amiga .MAP pitch (AGA, 7 bitplanes) to a Tiled .tmj map
SwosGfx -amiga -map -output=tmj -palette=Normal -bitplanes=7 SWCPICH1.MAP pitch1-normal-aga.tmj

```

# Trippples — An Abstract Strategy Game Revisited

**Trippples** (deliberately spelled with three *p*s) is an abstract strategy board game designed by William T. Powers in the early 1970s. This project explores the game through a modern, browser-based implementation, beginning with a playable proof of concept.

The long-term goal is to bring this unusual game to modern platforms while preserving its original character and documenting the reasoning behind the implementation.

## Why This Project?

This project has a personal history that goes back almost three decades.

Back in 1997, I discovered Paul Kienitz's Amiga implementation of Trippples in C on an old Amiga Public Domain disk, most likely from the Fred Fish collection. I liked the game enough to write my own DOS conversion in Turbo Pascal.

And then, as these things sometimes do, the project disappeared into the back of my mind.

Fast-forward to very recently, when I came across a paper printout of my old Pascal source code while clearing out some long-forgotten stuff in the attic. Seeing it again brought the game back to life in my mind. Somehow, it suddenly seemed obvious: **this game deserves a new life on a modern platform — perhaps even on a mobile phone.**

Rather than jumping straight into a full-blown application, I decided to start small and build a proof of concept first. The immediate goal is to get the rules right, establish a sound technical foundation, and make the game playable in a modern browser.

Partly, this is about bringing an old piece of personal computing history back to life. But it's also about revisiting something I created almost thirty years ago, understanding it again with today's tools, and seeing where the idea can go from here.

Some projects never quite leave you. They just wait patiently in the attic.

## The Game

Trippples is played on an 8×8 board containing directional tiles. Each directional tile displays three arrows pointing in directions chosen from the eight possible directions of movement.

Its defining mechanic is unusual: **the tile occupied by your opponent's piece determines your available movement directions.** You must therefore consider not only your own position and route, but also how your opponent's position affects your next move.

The board combines directional tiles with starting positions, destinations, and other special fields. Players navigate the board according to the movement rules and attempt to complete their route before their opponent.

The precise setup and some gameplay details differ between surviving descriptions and later computer implementations. Reconstructing and documenting the rules is therefore an integral part of the project.

## Current Implementation

The project currently consists of a browser-based proof of concept built with HTML, JavaScript, and Canvas.

The implementation is deliberately modular:

- **`board.js`** — board representation, tile data, and board-related helpers.
- **`rules.js`** — movement rules and legal-move calculations.
- **`rulesets.js`** — definitions of the available rulesets.
- **`game.js`** — game state, turn management, and game logic.
- **`ui.js`** — board rendering and user interaction.
- **`main.js`** — application initialization and coordination.

The underlying principle is to keep game rules, game state, and presentation separate, making the logic easier to test and the implementation easier to extend.

![Trippples game board](screenshots/scr01.jpg)
![Trippples game board](screenshots/scr02.jpg)

### Current Features

- An interactive 8×8 game board.
- Local human-versus-human gameplay.
- Two selectable rulesets: **Current Rules** and **Classic Rules**.
- Ruleset switching with confirmation before the current game is discarded.
- Drag-and-drop movement.
- Visual indication of the active player's position.
- Distinct visual representations for blocked fields and route objectives.
- Two compact player maps showing route progress and the next objective.
- A responsive layout designed to accommodate different screen sizes and arrangements.
- A lightweight browser-based test runner covering rules, game logic, and UI behaviour.

The two rulesets provide different board configurations and starting positions while sharing the same underlying movement and game infrastructure. This makes it possible to explore different interpretations without duplicating the core implementation.

The test runner helps verify the underlying logic independently of manually playing through the interface.

## Reconstructing the Rules

One of the main challenges is determining which rules belong to the original commercial game and which details may have changed in subsequent implementations.

The research draws on historical rule material, contemporary descriptions, and surviving computer implementations. The original rulebook and historical sources take priority when discrepancies arise, while the Amiga implementation provides a valuable reference for understanding how a complete digital version handles practical gameplay situations.

The project currently offers two explicitly defined configurations rather than silently combining incompatible interpretations. Their setup and gameplay implications are documented separately.

See the accompanying documentation:

- **[Sources & Reference Material](SOURCES.md)** — historical sources, implementations, and their relative reliability.
- **[Game Rules](GAME_RULES.md)** — the implemented rulesets, gameplay mechanics, implementation decisions, and unresolved discrepancies.
- **[Architecture](ARCHITECTURE.md)** — the code structure, responsibilities of individual modules, and design decisions.

## Architecture and Design Principles

The proof of concept is being developed with a few straightforward principles in mind:

- **Separation of concerns:** rules and game state should not depend on rendering or UI details.
- **Testable logic:** legal moves, turn transitions, and winning conditions should be verifiable without interacting with the board manually.
- **Explicit decisions:** uncertain rules and deviations from historical sources should be documented.
- **Flexible presentation:** the board and supporting controls should adapt to different layouts instead of relying on fixed positioning.
- **Reusable rulesets:** alternative board configurations should use the same underlying game engine wherever possible.
- **Incremental development:** establish correct local gameplay before introducing networking or platform-specific features.

These principles are intended to keep the project understandable and maintainable as it grows.

## Future Direction

The current browser version is a foundation, not the final product.

The longer-term plan is to explore an Android version with online, turn-based multiplayer. A possible architecture would combine a REST API for conventional requests with WebSockets for real-time communication and turn updates.

Other areas for future investigation include:

- A computer opponent based on minimax search with alpha-beta pruning.
- Server-side move validation for online games.
- Adapting the game and its interface to mobile devices.

These are planned directions, not features of the current proof of concept. The immediate priority remains a sound, well-tested implementation of the game itself.

## Historical References

The following sources form the basis of the rule reconstruction:

- [Tripppin — Amiga implementation by Paul Kienitz](https://github.com/paulkienitz/Tripppin)
- [BoardGameGeek — Trippples](https://boardgamegeek.com/boardgame/2040/trippples)
- [Abstract Games — Issue 7 (PDF)](https://www.abstractgames.org/uploads/1/1/6/4/116462923/abstract_games_issue_7.pdf)
- [Original Trippples English rulebook (PDF)](https://tesera.ru/images/items/905121/Trippples%20ENG.pdf)
- [Don's Game Closet — Game Rules](https://www.donsgamecloset.com/GameRulesTpU.html)

For detailed notes on these references and the questions they raise, see [SOURCES.md](SOURCES.md).

---

*Trippples is an independent, exploratory software project inspired by a historical board game. The project is not affiliated with the original designer or publishers.*
